holidays.name: Bathtub Party Day
holidays.description: Fill the tub, grab your rubber ducky, and invite the bubbles. Today is an excuse to turn bath time into a full-on soggy soirée. Bring snacks, a good playlist, and maybe a few friends in swimsuits if space allows.
holidays.origin: An unofficial observance of unclear origin, often linked to the date Prohibition ended. It plays on the Prohibition-era legend of bathtub gin.
holidays.funFact: Bathtub gin got its name because bottles were often too tall to be filled from the sink tap, so people mixed the spirit in jugs under the faucet or in the tub.

holidays.name: National Sacher Torte Day
holidays.description: A day to indulge in Vienna's most famous chocolate cake. It has dense chocolate sponge, a thin layer of apricot jam, and a glossy chocolate glaze. It is traditionally served with unsweetened whipped cream.
holidays.origin: Franz Sacher created the dessert in Vienna in 1832 when he was a 16-year-old apprentice cook. He was making dessert for Prince Metternich's guests. The cake later sparked a famous legal dispute between the Hotel Sacher and the Demel bakery over who could call theirs the 'original'.
holidays.funFact: The Sacher torte feud between Hotel Sacher and Demel lasted for years. It ended with a court ruling that let the hotel advertise its cake as the 'Original Sacher-Torte'.

holidays.name: National Repeal Day
holidays.description: Raise a glass to the end of Prohibition. This day marks the moment America's 13-year ban on alcohol ended. Many people mark it with a classic cocktail and a toast to speakeasy history.
holidays.origin: On December 5, 1933, Utah became the 36th state to ratify the 21st Amendment. That gave the amendment the three-fourths majority it needed, and it repealed the 18th Amendment.
holidays.funFact: The 21st Amendment is the only amendment ever ratified to repeal another one. It is also the only one approved by state ratifying conventions instead of state legislatures.
